deep.reconstruction:
Folio 8r is a compact formula sheet headed 'Formeln der sphaerischen Trigonometrie. Allgemeine' (general, oblique triangles). It continues f.7v (plane trigonometry) and precedes f.8v (right-angled spherical triangles). Notation: a, b, c are the sides and A, B, C the opposite angles. There are no worked derivations; the bridging steps below are mine.

(1)* cos a = cos b cos c + sin b sin c cos A. This is the side cosine law.

(2) da = cos C db + cos B dc + sin B sin c dA. This is the total differential of a as a function of (b, c, A). My derivation: differentiating (1) gives -sin a da = (cos b sin c cos A - sin b cos c) db + (sin b cos c cos A - cos b sin c) dc - sin b sin c sin A dA. By the five-part formula, sin b cos c - cos b sin c cos A = sin a cos C, and similarly for c. By the sine law, sin b sin A = sin a sin B. Dividing by -sin a gives (2).

(3) sin a cos B = cos b sin c - sin b cos c cos A. This is the five-part (analogue) formula.

(4)* sin a sin B = sin b sin A. This is the sine law.

(5) cot a da - cot A dA = cot b db - cot B dB. This is the logarithmic differential of (4), rearranged (mine): cot a da + cot B dB = cot b db + cot A dA.

(6)* cos A cos c = cot b sin c - cot B sin A. This is the four-part (cotangent) formula. The small numerals 2 3 / 1 3 4 2 under it number the four consecutive parts: b=1 (outer side), A=2 (inner angle), c=3 (inner side), B=4 (outer angle). The formula then reads cos(2)cos(3) = cot(1)sin(3) - cot(4)sin(2), a mnemonic.

(7) sin C db = sin b cos C dA + cos a sin B dc + sin a dB. This is the differential of side b in terms of (A, c, B), i.e. the ASA data. My derivation: start from the cyclic variant of (10), sin C sin a db = dB + cos a dC + cos c dA. Eliminate dC with dC = -cos b dA - cos a dB + sin A sin b dc. Use cos c - cos a cos b = sin a sin b cos C and sin A sin b = sin a sin B, then divide by sin a.

(8) sin A cos b = cos B sin C + sin B cos C cos a. This is the polar (dual) of (3), obtained by a -> pi-A, A -> pi-a, etc.

(9)* cos A = -cos B cos C + sin B sin C cos a. This is the angle cosine law, the polar of (1).

(10) dA = -cos c dB - cos b dC + sin B sin c da. This is the polar of (2). The polar transformation gives the coefficient sin b sin C, which equals sin B sin c by the sine law.

(11) sin(A/2) = sqrt(sin((a+b-c)/2) sin((a-b+c)/2)/(sin b sin c)) and cos(A/2) = sqrt(sin((a+b+c)/2) sin((b+c-a)/2)/(sin b sin c)). These are the half-angle formulas, i.e. sqrt(sin(s-b)sin(s-c)/(sin b sin c)) and sqrt(sin s sin(s-a)/(sin b sin c)). They are the spherical analogues of (5) and (6) on the previous page.

(12) The four 'Gauss analogies':
- cos(A/2) sin((b-c)/2) = sin((B-C)/2) sin(a/2)
- sin(A/2) sin((b+c)/2) = cos((B-C)/2) sin(a/2)
- cos(A/2) cos((b-c)/2) = sin((B+C)/2) cos(a/2)
- sin(A/2) cos((b+c)/2) = cos((B+C)/2) cos(a/2)

Purpose: a reference sheet for astronomical and geodetic computation. Asterisks mark the four fundamental relations. The differential formulas serve error propagation and correction of observations.
errors: None found: every formula checks out, including the three differential relations and the four Gauss analogies.
The coefficient of da in (10) appears as sin B sin c, whereas direct polar transformation of (2) gives sin b sin C. These are equal by the sine law, so this is not an error.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard compendium of spherical trigonometry formulas, all correct. The only item associated with Gauss, the 'Gauss analogies', is already published in Theoria motus (1809) and attributed to him (with Delambre's priority known). The neatly organized differential formulas and the four-part mnemonic are textbook material of the time.

transcription_corrections: In the formula 'sin A cos b = cos B sin C + ...', the 'sin' before C is written over an earlier word (overstrike), and the final 'cos a' is partly obscured. The reading cos B sin C + sin B cos C cos a is mathematically correct.
In 'cotg b . ∂b' the ∂b is heavily re-inked (corrected), not a different symbol.
The numerals under the four-part formula (2 3 / 1 3 4 2) are a mnemonic numbering of the consecutive parts b=1, A=2, c=3, B=4, not exponents or footnotes.
The folio marks read: circled '(8)', then '48/4' struck through, then '8'.
